As Fanny already shared, to move from concept to action, The Working Group established a roadmap and launched a country mapping exercise to better understand the current state of gender and energy data and identify critical gaps. This mapping follows an agreed framework based on two core dimensions. The first is energy access. Clean energy mitigates health risks for women, reduces time poverty resulting from unpaid care work, and opens pathways to entrepreneurship and livelihoods. For the energy sector, engaging women as consumers and clean energy providers unlocks market growth and provides vital user insights. The second dimension is economic opportunities. For an energy sector facing labor bottlenecks, Increasing women's participation— and women currently make up less than 5% of the technical workforce— will help bridge critical skill gaps and drive innovation. Yet, as the policy brief highlights, despite these clear interlinkages, SDG 7 currently lacks a dedicated gender indicator to measure and track these critical dimensions. To identify practical pathways for strengthening gender matrixes in the energy sector, we began by asking a simple question: What data do countries already collect? Using a replicable country mapping methodology, we reviewed national data systems across a growing number of countries. What we discovered is a defined data paradox. The data exists, but it remains largely invisible. Across many countries, standard national surveys already collect the raw information needed to measure key aspects of energy access and the participation in the energy workforce. The underlying datasets contain variables that can be analyzed by sex, and used to generate valuable gender insights. However, these opportunities are rarely reflected in official reporting. In many cases, we find that the data that could be sex disaggregated rarely is analyzed or reported in that way. And where reporting does take place, the absence of common standards results in significant inconsistencies across countries. This finding has important strategic implications. It suggests that the gender data gap is not primarily a data collecting— data collection challenge. Rather, it is an analysis, disaggregation, and reporting challenge. This insight opens a pragmatic way forward, leveraging existing statistical infrastructure which is— we will try to demonstrate in the next two slides. Because countries rarely report sex-disaggregated data on electricity access, we analyze microdata from 30 recent demographic and health surveys to demonstrate the type of insights that are already available within existing data. For electricity access, the direction and magnitude of gender gaps vary significantly across countries. And my apologies that the slide is small, but we will make these slides available for all of you to read. For example, in Ethiopia, female-headed households hold a distinct advantage with nearly 13 percentage points higher electrification rates. Co-conversely, in Angola, male-headed households lead by nearly 10% points. We also examined appliance ownership, which provides a more nuanced picture of how electricity is actually used. Male-headed households typically dominated ownership of entertainment assets such as televisions, while female-headed households showed a stronger tendency towards domestic appliances such as refrigerators. These results align closely with the development literature illustrating how intra-household resource allocation reflects gender divisions of labor and differentiating asset priorities. Next slide, please. Similarly, employment in the energy sector is not systematically disaggregated by sex. However, our mapping exercise captured countries that do report it. As shown on the slide, indicators vary across countries. Countries may report multiple indicators based on different data sources, for example, household labor surveys or enterprise surveys. Data is most often categorized under the broad industrial classifications of electricity, gas, steam, and air conditioning supply. Finally, one important gap to highlight from the findings of the country mapping is that data on employment in the renewable energy sector is still scarce. Next slide, please. In conclusion, allow me to convey three key takeaways from the country mapping. First, the headline finding from our work is that the challenge is not the lack of primary data collection. The foundations are already there. Countries are collecting much of the information needed to measure the links between gender and clean energy. Second, what is missing is the systematic analysis, sex disaggregation, and upward reporting of this data. Third, this insight reframes our solution. We must leverage existing national surveys and pair them with clear reporting standards. Moving into our next phase, the working group's operational agenda is: expanding the MICMEC exercise to 50 priority countries while finalizing and validating all country profiles with national experts and institutions, capturing missing dimensions, particularly by exploring ways to incorporate women's agency and decision-making into the data, and deliver a global synthesis note that summarizes the key trends, common indicators, and initial data gaps across all 50 countries. Also, a Commission-endorsed methodology will enable UNST to carry out methodological training to countries. With all these in place, we'll be well positioned to advocate for specific indicators to inform the important topic of gender and energy.

Thank you so much, Professor. Well, our session would not be complete without hearing from young voices. I'm pleased to introduce Mr. Josh Oxbey, Global Focal Point for the SDG 7 Youth Constituency. Agency. Over to you, Josh.

Thank you, Chair. Um, yeah, let me start by saying that I think data can sound really technical, um, it can sound neutral, and it can sound administrative. But in the context of energy, as we've all heard today, data decides who is visible, who's protected, and who's still left out systems altogether. When we talk about moving from a 'call to count' sort of as the framing of the session is today, I think we have to push this narrative one step further because gender-disaggregated energy data isn't only a reporting issue, it's a question of power. Power in the household, power in policy, and ultimately power in deciding what the energy transition is actually for. I think that's why this HLPF can't just be treated as as another progress check. So we know it's the final one before 2030. But at this stage, the numbers are not only telling us whether SDG 7 is moving, they're exposing what the framework still struggles to see. Because 4 years out from 2030, the uncomfortable truth is that some gaps aren't moving, they're concentrating. Some inequalities aren't being solved, they're being hidden behind averages. And from a youth perspective, that's the real test for what comes next. Not only what the SDGs delivered, but whether the future development goals will be brave enough to measure what the SDGs left behind. Which is why I want to kind of highlight 3 points from our global youth perspective on how gender-disaggregated data can move from visibility to delivery. First, Gender energy data can help us move from access to agency. We've all heard this here today. A household connection doesn't tell us who controls the energy use inside of a home. Clean cooking statistics don't tell us whether women and girls have gained time, safety, health, and income. And electricity access figures don't tell us whether energy is affordable, reliable, meaningful, or useful enough to support learning, enterprise, and decent work. That's one of the real use cases of gender data that I see, helping us to see whether energy access is becoming empowerment or whether we're simply just electrifying inequality. My second point: gender and youth data must connect skills to real jobs. One of the reflections I've just taken away from London Climate Action Week just there is that we're seeing that the energy transition is increasingly being directed by the systems around energy: finance, skills, infrastructure, labor market statistics. Gender-disaggregated data then can't simply sit at the edge of energy conversations. It has to cut through all of those systems. It should shape where finance goes, how projects are designed, who gets trained, who moves from informal community energy work into decent work, because future jobs are already being promised. But without that data, we simply can't tell whether those jobs are going to become pathways for young women and girls or another closed door with a better branding. My third point is that youth organizations, women's groups, and academia can really help turn data into accountability. We can help show that what national averages miss— who pays for energy, who loses time when it fails, and who's still invisible. In the data. That evidence has to move into national energy plans, project design, procurement rules, and sort of this post-2030 framework narrative that we're all pushing here today. Because if what gets financed actually gets done, then what gets measured shapes what gets financed. And that for me is the real challenge in the final 4 years to 2030 and for the future development goals that come after it. Gender disaggregated data can't sit at the margins of SDG 7 as a technical add-on. It has to become a part of how we understand whether energy access is actually delivering agency, affordability, productive youth use, decent work and leadership. And for young people, that distinction really matters because visibility isn't the same as a voice. Participation isn't the same as power. And inclusion isn't the same as accountability. So as we move from the SDGs to the FTGs, the next generation of energy policy really has to tell the truth about delivery. Who benefits? Who's left out? Who carries the burden and what needs to change? Not just counting women and young people in the transition, but making it near impossible to design, finance, or report on the future of the transition without them. Thank you.
